question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer: No. When a creature phases back in, that does not count as it entering the battlefield, so "enters the battlefield" triggered abilities do not trigger. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that the phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, and that "zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Since enters-the-battlefield abilities are a type of zone-change trigger (as described in [603.6a]), phasing in specifically does not cause them to fire. Instead, the permanent's status simply changes back to "phased in" and the game once again treats it as though it exists on the battlefield ([702.26c]), but this is not treated as a new arrival. Note also that effects that check a phased-in permanent's history won't treat the phasing event as having caused it to leave or enter the battlefield ([702.26d]), so even "the first time this creature enters the battlefield this turn"-style checks aren't triggered or reset by phasing. Similarly, attached/unattached triggers don't fire on phasing either ([702.26j]), which reinforces the general principle that phasing is not treated like a normal zone change for triggered-ability purposes. This holds the same in both two-player and multiplayer games, since these phasing rules aren't framed as two-player-specific (though multiplayer has extra wrinkles, e.g. [702.26n], about permanents that phased out under a player who then left the game).

Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, the deathtouch ability changes what counts as "lethal damage" for trample's damage-assignment rules, letting the attacker assign only 1 damage to each blocking creature and send the rest through to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking.

Here's why: Trample (rule 702.19a) is a static ability that modifies how an attacking creature assigns its combat damage. Under rule 702.19b, the controller of an attacking creature with trample must first assign lethal damage to each blocking creature before assigning any excess damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle. Normally "lethal damage" means damage equal to or greater than the blocking creature's toughness (see the definition of Lethal Damage, referencing rules 120.4a, 120.6, 510.1, and 704.5g).

But deathtouch changes that calculation. Rule 702.2c states that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purpose of determining whether excess damage is being dealt. Rule 120.4a echoes this: any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source has deathtouch. So when the attacking creature has deathtouch, its controller only needs to assign 1 damage to a blocking creature to satisfy the "lethal damage" requirement of rule 702.19b — everything beyond that 1 point is excess and can be assigned to the blocking creature(s), the defending player, or a planeswalker/battle being attacked, at the attacking player's choice.

Once that 1 damage (or more, if the controller chooses to assign more) is dealt and marked on the blocking creature, rule 704.5h (and rule 702.2b) makes that creature destroyed as a state-based action, since it has toughness greater than 0 and has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last state-based action check — regardless of whether the damage marked actually reaches its toughness value.

If the attacker is blocked by multiple creatures, the same logic applies to each: only 1 damage needs to be assigned to each blocker to treat it as having received lethal damage, per rule 702.19b, before the rest tramples over.

Note: this is a two-player-style example as framed by the rules given (attacker vs. single defending player/planeswalker), but nothing about how trample+deathtouch interacts changes in a multiplayer game — the same assignment rules in 702.19b and 702.2c apply regardless of how many players are at the table; the only multiplayer-specific consideration would be which player/planeswalker/battle is being attacked, which isn't affected by deathtouch.

When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. The attacking creature’s controller need not assign lethal damage to all those blocking creatures but in that case can’t assign any damage to the player or planeswalker it’s attacking. The attacking creature’s controller can divide the rest of the damage as they choose between the blocking creature and the defending player.

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes, Storm is a triggered ability, and like other triggered abilities it can be countered — but only by an effect that specifically says it counters abilities, not by an effect that only counters spells.

Storm is defined as "a triggered ability that functions on the stack" [702.40a]: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn..." Because it's a triggered ability, once it triggers it's put on the stack as a separate object, distinct from the spell itself [603.3, 603.3d]. Per rule [113.9], "Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, and therefore can't be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities." So a card that says "counter target spell" cannot stop the Storm trigger (it could only counter the spell itself, e.g., before Storm triggers or resolves), but a card that says "counter target activated or triggered ability" (or similarly worded) can counter the Storm trigger, preventing the copies from being made. Note that even if the Storm trigger itself resolves and makes copies, those copies are themselves spells on the stack and can then be countered normally by spell-countering effects.

This holds the same whether you're playing with two players or more than one opponent — nothing about priority for multiplayer changes how the Storm trigger goes on the stack or how it can be countered.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer: No. A card with a hybrid mana symbol is considered to be all of the colors that make up that symbol, not just one of them. Rule 107.4e states: "A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors," and rule 202.2d confirms that "an object with one or more hybrid mana symbols ... in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols." That means a card with, say, {R/G} in its mana cost or rules text has both red AND green in its color identity (per rule 903.4, color identity comes from the colors of any mana symbols in the mana cost or rules text). Under the Commander deck-building rule 903.5c, a card can only go in your deck if EVERY color in its color identity is also in your commander's color identity. So if your commander's color identity is only red (no green), a card containing {R/G} is illegal for your deck, because its green component isn't covered. The same logic is spelled out for monocolored hybrid symbols like {2/W} - they still count as that one color, so a {2/W} card needs white in the commander's identity too. Bottom line: you can only include a hybrid-symbol card if your commander's color identity contains ALL of the colors in that hybrid symbol, not just one of them.

(Most cards with hybrid mana symbols in their mana costs are printed in a two-tone frame. See rule 107.4e.)

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. You cannot respond to anything happening in the untap step because no player receives priority during that step at all. Rule [502.4] states that no player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or resolve and no abilities can be activated or resolved during it. Rule [117.3a] confirms this explicitly: "No player receives priority during the untap step."

What actually happens in the untap step are turn-based actions, which don't use the stack and happen automatically: phasing out/in of the active player's permanents with phasing [502.1][703.4a], the day/night designation check [731.2], and the active player untapping their permanents [703.4c]. Because none of these use the stack, there's no opportunity to respond to them.

If any ability triggers during the untap step (for example, from the phasing action), it doesn't go on the stack immediately. Instead, per [502.4] and [503.1a], it's held until the next time a player would receive priority — normally the upkeep step, when the active player gets priority and any abilities that triggered during the untap step (or at the beginning of upkeep) are put onto the stack first. So you can respond to those triggered abilities once they're on the stack in the upkeep step, but not during the untap step itself.

This holds true regardless of how many players are in the game — none of the rules governing the untap step (502.4, 703.4a/c, 731.2) differentiate between two-player and multiplayer games; the untap step is always a no-priority step for every player at the table.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer: Yes. A creature remains an attacking creature throughout the end of combat step. Per the definition of Attacking Creature and rule [508.1k], a creature "remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first." The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase, not a separate phase, so simply entering that step does not end the combat phase and does not remove creatures from combat. Rule [511.3] confirms this explicitly: "As soon as the end of combat step ends, all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat. After the end of combat step ends, the combat phase is over and the postcombat main phase begins." This is also why "at end of combat" triggered abilities (rule [511.2]) fire as the end of combat step *begins* — they need the creatures to still be attacking/blocking at that moment to have a meaningful trigger event, and effects that reference an attacking creature and its defending player (rule [508.5]) still function normally during this step. Removal from combat before the step ends can still happen for other reasons listed in rule [506.4a] (e.g., the creature leaves the battlefield, changes controller, phases out, stops being a creature, etc.), but simply being in the end of combat step does not by itself remove a creature from combat. Note: one specific effect (Mandate of Peace) can end the combat phase early via rule [724.2d]/[724.2e], which does remove all creatures from combat immediately and even skips the end of combat step's triggers — but absent such an effect, creatures stay "attacking" through the normal end of combat step.

question: Do you cast lands?
answer: No. Playing a land is a special action, not casting a spell. Rule [305.1] states that a player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty, and specifically notes that "playing a land is a special action; it doesn't use the stack." Because it never goes on the stack, a land is never a spell — rule [305.1] and [505.6b] both make clear that "neither the land nor the action of playing the land is a spell or ability, so it can't be countered, and players can't respond to it with instants or activated abilities." question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. Once the evoke triggered ability is on the stack, you get a chance to sacrifice the evoked creature by other means (such as an activated sacrifice ability) before that triggered ability resolves.

Here's why: Evoke works by creating a triggered ability that reads "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" [702.74a]. When that permanent enters the battlefield, the ability triggers, and it's put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3d]. Once it's on the stack, the game doesn't resolve it immediately — players pass priority in succession before anything on top of the stack resolves [608.1]. During that priority window, any player (most relevantly you, as the creature's controller) can activate an ability whose cost is sacrificing a creature, and you could choose to sacrifice the evoked creature to that ability while the evoke trigger is still sitting on the stack unresolved.

If you do this, when the evoke triggered ability finally resolves, its instruction "its controller sacrifices it" refers back to the permanent that was its source. Under rule [113.7a], if that source (the evoked creature) is no longer in the zone it's expected to be in — here, the battlefield, because you already sacrificed it — the ability uses the creature's last known information, but the sacrifice action can't actually happen again since the creature has already left the battlefield. In practice, the evoke trigger simply does nothing at that point; the creature isn't sacrificed twice, and you don't get any double benefit from 'dying' twice — but you have successfully fed it to whatever other sacrifice outlet you used first, and any abilities that care about that other sacrifice (e.g., an exploit or reflexive trigger tied to that specific sacrifice) will have seen the evoke creature die from your chosen outlet rather than from the evoke ability itself.

This holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since nothing about priority or triggered-ability stacking in the rules cited here changes with player count.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. Keyword abilities are still abilities, so an effect that says a permanent "loses all abilities" removes its keyword abilities along with any other abilities it has.

Rule [702.1] explains that a keyword like "flying" or "trample" is just a rules-shorthand name for an ability that would otherwise need to be spelled out in full rules text — it is not a separate category from "ability." Rule [113.10] (and its sub-rule [113.10b]) says that effects which remove abilities remove all instances of the specified ability, and "loses all abilities" removes every ability the object has, whether it's a keyword, a granted ability, or a written-out ability. Rule [613.1f] confirms this operates in Layer 6 of the continuous-effects system, where ability-adding and ability-removing effects (including keyword counters) are applied.

One caveat: characteristic-defining abilities (rule [604.3]) are a special case — they define an object's characteristics (like power/toughness) rather than functioning as a normal granted ability, but a "loses all abilities" effect still removes them as abilities per the general rule; the rules text given doesn't carve out an exception for CDAs from a "loses all abilities" effect. Also note rule [603.6d]'s example: if "All creatures lose all abilities" applies to a creature as it enters the battlefield, that creature's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability (itself often paired with keyword-like abilities) simply won't trigger — reinforcing that "loses all abilities" is comprehensive and includes keyword abilities.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. There is no rule that stops you from drawing cards just because you're at your maximum hand size. A player may have any number of cards in hand at any time during the game — the maximum hand size only matters as a turn-based action during the active player's cleanup step, when the active player discards down to their maximum hand size (normally seven) [402.2] [514.1] [703.4n]. Drawing itself is never restricted by hand size; the only time excess cards get removed is in that cleanup-step check, and even then only if it's still true when the cleanup step begins.

So you can keep drawing cards well past seven (or whatever your maximum is) all through your turn and your opponents' turns. If you're the active player and you still have more cards than your maximum when your cleanup step begins, you'll have to discard down to that number at that point [703.4n]. If a hand-size modifying effect (like a vanguard card's hand modifier) changes your maximum hand size, that adjusted number is what you'd eventually discard down to [313.6] [902.5b].

One caveat unrelated to hand size: if you're required to draw more cards than remain in your library, you draw what's left and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority [104.3c] — but that's about library size, not hand size.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
If a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters on it (loyalty can't be reduced below 0 - see below), it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically the next time state-based actions are checked, before any player would receive priority; it doesn't use the stack and no one needs to respond to it.

A few things to unpack: Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have, and the loyalty of a planeswalker on the battlefield is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it [306.5c]. Loyalty counters are markers placed on the planeswalker, and "a planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action" [122.1e, 306.9]. This specific state-based action is listed explicitly: "If a planeswalker has loyalty 0, it's put into its owner's graveyard" [704.5i]. State-based actions are checked and performed automatically whenever the game state meets the listed conditions, and they don't use the stack [704.1].

Regarding "0 or less": loyalty counters, like other counters, cannot go negative - if a planeswalker takes damage (which removes that many loyalty counters, per rules 120.3c and 306.8) equal to or greater than its current loyalty, all of its loyalty counters are simply removed, leaving it at 0 loyalty. There's no such thing as a planeswalker sitting at, say, -2 loyalty; it just hits 0 and is then put into its owner's graveyard by the state-based action described above. So functionally, "0 or less" and "exactly 0" loyalty counters lead to the same outcome.

This is a single-player-independent rule (it doesn't depend on how many players are in the game), so it applies the same way in both two-player and multiplayer games.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. In the strict rules sense, only creatures and planeswalkers can "die." Rule 700.4 defines: "The term dies means 'is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.'" The glossary entry for Dies is even more specific: "A creature or planeswalker 'dies' if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield." A non-creature artifact (one that isn't also a creature) is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so when it's put into its owner's graveyard from the battlefield, that event is not called "dying" in the rules' technical sense — it's simply being destroyed, sacrificed, or otherwise put into the graveyard.

That said, this is purely a matter of terminology, not of function: the artifact still leaves the battlefield and ends up in the graveyard just like a creature would. Rule 701.8b explains a permanent is only "destroyed" via an effect that says "destroy" or via the lethal-damage/deathtouch state-based actions (704.5g, 704.5h) — those state-based actions only apply to creatures anyway, so a non-creature artifact can't be destroyed by lethal damage in the first place; it's normally destroyed by an explicit "destroy" effect, sacrificed (per the Sacrifice rule and 701.21), or put into the graveyard some other way.

Importantly, abilities don't need the word "dies" to react to an artifact leaving the battlefield: a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability written as "Whenever this artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield..." or "When this artifact leaves the battlefield..." still works fine on a non-creature artifact, per rule 603.6c, and such zone-change triggers "look back in time" per rule 603.10a. It's only wording that specifically keys off "dies" (e.g., "Whenever a creature dies") that won't be triggered by a non-creature artifact going to the graveyard, precisely because dying is defined as something only creatures and planeswalkers do.

Note: if an artifact happens to also be a creature (an artifact creature), then it IS a creature, so it does die when put into the graveyard from the battlefield — the "non-creature" qualifier in your question is the key distinction.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose the game instantly at the moment of the failed draw — instead you lose as a state-based action the next time any player would receive priority. Under rule [121.4], "A player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority." This is implemented as the state-based action described in [704.5b]: "If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game." State-based actions themselves don't use the stack and are checked automatically whenever the game would otherwise give a player priority [704.1].

If you were required to draw more cards than remain in your library (e.g., an effect says "draw three cards" but you only have one left), you draw whatever cards are actually there and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority — per [104.3c]: "If a player is required to draw more cards than are left in their library, they draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority." This is consistent with the general rule [609.3] that an effect which attempts something impossible does as much as possible.

A few related wrinkles worth knowing: if an effect merely offers you the *choice* to draw while your library is empty, you can still choose to do so — the empty library doesn't stop the choice [121.3, 121.3a]. And if a replacement effect modifies your draw (e.g., "if you would draw a card, instead..."), that replacement still applies even though there's no card to draw [121.6a] [614.11]. Also, moving cards to your hand without using the word "draw" isn't a draw for these purposes and won't trigger the empty-library loss on its own [121.5].

This all applies regardless of how many players are in the game — the rules cited (121.4, 704.5b, 104.3c) aren't framed as two-player-specific and describe a state-based action that checks each player's library independently, so the same mechanic applies at a multiplayer table without any special exception noted in the provided rules.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the draw attempt happens as a normal turn-based action in your draw step [504.1, 121.1] or as part of resolving a spell/ability's draw instruction. If instead the empty-library draw happened earlier and you're now asking whether some intervening event could have saved you, the loss is still only applied via the state-based action check — so if your library were somehow refilled before the next state-based action check, rule 704.5b's language ("attempted to draw...since the last time state-based actions were checked") would still flag the earlier attempt, since the rule cares about the attempt having occurred, not your library's current count. But that specific edge case isn't further detailed in the rules provided beyond this wording.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
Steps in combat (rule 506.1): beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. If no creatures are declared as attackers (or put onto the battlefield attacking), the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped [508.8]. If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps [506.1].

As the defending player, here's when you get priority:

- In a two-player game you are automatically the defending player just by being the nonactive player during the combat phase [506.2/506.2a] — no choice is made about who defends. In a multiplayer game, unless the variant makes all of the attacking player's opponents defending players automatically (as with the Attack Multiple Players option, rule 802.2, where all opponents become defending players), the attacking player chooses one opponent as defending player as a turn-based action at the very start of the beginning of combat step, before anyone gets priority [507.1, 703.4h].

- At the start of each step and phase, once any turn-based actions for that step have been handled and any triggered abilities that trigger 'at the beginning of' that step have been put on the stack, the *active* player receives priority first, not you [117.3a]. Only the player with priority may cast spells or activate abilities [117.1]. As the defending (nonactive) player, you get your chance to act after the active player has priority and passes it — the provided rules confirm the active player goes first in each step but don't include the specific rule describing exactly how priority passes from one player to the next, so I can't cite the mechanics of that hand-off beyond 'active player first, then it moves on.'

- In the combat damage step specifically, both damage assignment and dealing damage are turn-based actions that don't use the stack: the active player announces how their attacking creatures assign damage, then you (the defending player) announce how your blocking creatures assign damage [510.1, 703.4k]; then all assigned damage is dealt simultaneously with no opportunity for either player to cast spells or activate abilities in between [510.2]. Only after damage is dealt does the active player receive priority, and then it would pass to you.

- The end of combat step has no turn-based actions at all; once it begins, the active player simply receives priority [511.1], and again it would subsequently pass to you.

- In multiplayer games with more than one defending player, combat damage assignment happens in APNAP (active player, then non-active players in turn order) order, but otherwise proceeds like the two-player case [802.5].

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No — you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities (activated or triggered) never use the stack, so they resolve immediately as they're activated/triggered rather than waiting for priority, and by definition they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to [113.4] [605.3b] [605.4a]. Since nothing ever exists on the stack for opponents (or even the controller) to respond to, priority simply returns to whoever had it before the mana ability was used, after the ability has already resolved [405.6c].

This applies to both activated mana abilities (like tapping a land for mana) and triggered mana abilities (like an effect that triggers off tapping a land and adds bonus mana) [605.3b] [605.4a]. Note the special rule for split second: even while a spell with split second is on the stack, players may still activate mana abilities, but still can't respond to them since they bypass the stack entirely [702.61b].

One caveat: an ability that could produce mana but requires a target, or a triggered ability that triggers from something other than the activation of a mana ability, is NOT actually a mana ability under the rules — it follows normal activated/triggered ability rules and DOES use the stack, meaning it CAN be responded to [605.5a]. So the real test is whether the ability meets the mana-ability criteria (no target, could add mana on resolution, not a loyalty ability for activated abilities) [605.1a] — if it does, it's unresponsive; if it doesn't (e.g., it has a target), it behaves like any other ability and is open to responses.

This holds true regardless of how many players are in the game — the stack-avoidance and no-response rule for genuine mana abilities is not affected by player count.

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not itself an action that uses the stack, and no player receives priority while a cost is being paid, so there is no window in which another player can "respond" to that specific payment. Casting a spell or activating an ability follows a fixed sequence (proposal, cost determination/locking, then payment) under rules 601.2f–601.2h, and this entire sequence happens before the spell or ability is complete and before any player gets priority to act. Similarly, when declaring attackers or blockers, any required mana costs are paid as part of that turn-based action, which also doesn't use the stack (rules 508.1i, 508.1j, 509.1e, 509.1f). Because the total cost is "locked in" once it's determined (rule 601.2f), and because activating a cost-altering ability doesn't retroactively affect a spell or ability already on the stack (rule 602.4), you can't jump in with an instant or ability to change or interfere with a cost mid-payment — the payment either succeeds as locked in or, if it can't be completed, the whole action is reversed under rule 733.1.

What you *can* do is respond to the spell or ability itself once it has finished being cast/activated and is sitting on the stack (or, for turn-based actions like declaring attackers/blockers, once that step is complete and players get priority afterward). At that point you can cast instants or activate abilities in response to the spell/ability, but this doesn't let you undo or modify the cost that was already paid — it only lets you respond to the object now on the stack or to the game state resulting from the completed action. The one exception during payment itself is that the player actually paying a mana cost gets a chance to activate their own mana abilities as part of paying (rule 118.2), but that's the payer's own action, not a response by another player.

This answer assumes a normal two-player or multiplayer game; none of the provided rules distinguish two-player from multiplayer for this particular mechanic (cost payment not using the stack), so the answer is the same regardless of player count.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
The "layer system" is the procedure Magic uses to determine an object's final characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, abilities, etc.) whenever multiple continuous effects are affecting it at once. Rule [613.1] explains that you start with the object's actual (printed, or created) characteristics and then apply all applicable continuous effects in a fixed sequence of layers.

The layers are, in order:
- **Layer 1 (Copiable values):** Rules and effects that modify copiable values, such as copy effects and merging with permanents ([613.1a], [613.2a]). This layer itself has sublayers (1a is copy effects; timestamp order and dependency apply within it, [613.2c]). After layer 1 is fully applied, the object's characteristics are considered its "copiable values" ([613.2c], [707.2]).
- **Layer 2 (Control-changing effects):** effects that change who controls the object (implied by the Act of Treason example in [613.6], which places "gain control" in layer 2).
- **Layer 3 (Text-changing effects):** effects that change an object's rules text ([613.1c]).
- **Layer 4 (Type-changing effects):** effects that change card type, subtype, or supertype ([613.1d]).
- **Layer 5 (Color-changing effects):** effects that change color ([613.1e]).
- **Layer 6 (Ability-adding/removing effects, keyword counters, "can't have an ability" effects):** ([613.1f]).
- **Layer 7 (Power/toughness):** This layer has its own sublayers, applied in order: 7a is characteristic-defining abilities that set power/toughness ([613.4a] and [604.3]), 7b is effects that set power/toughness to a specific value, and 7c is effects that modify power/toughness (without setting it) such as +1/+1 counters or "gets +X/+X" effects — these sublayers are shown in the worked examples in [613.5] and [613.6].

Within most layers (2 through 6), effects from characteristic-defining abilities are applied first, then all other effects in timestamp order ([613.3]). Within layer 7's sublayers and layer 1's sublayers, effects are also applied in timestamp order ([613.2c], [613.4a], [613.7]) — an effect with an earlier timestamp applies before one with a later timestamp.

Two special rules can override or interact with straightforward layer/timestamp application:
- **Dependency ([613.8], [613.8a]):** Within a single layer or sublayer, if applying one effect would change the text, existence, targets, or result of another effect (and neither or both are characteristic-defining abilities), the first effect "depends on" the second, and dependency overrides the normal timestamp order.
- **Effects that span multiple layers ([613.6]):** A single effect can have parts that apply in different layers. question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action: if the same player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name at the same time, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others go to their owners' graveyards [704.5j][Legend Rule]. Any permanent with the supertype "legendary" is subject to this rule [205.4d], and since a rules change, planeswalker cards printed before the change now have the legendary supertype and are also subject to it (the old separate "planeswalker uniqueness rule" no longer exists) [306.4].

Key mechanics of how it works:
- It's a state-based action, so it doesn't use the stack and isn't something players do in response to — it just happens automatically whenever state-based actions are checked, which occurs every time before a player would receive priority [704.1][117.2d][117.5].
- It only applies to legendary permanents with the *exact same name* that are controlled by the *same player*. If two different players each control a legendary permanent with the same name, the rule doesn't apply to either of them, since each player only controls one copy.
- When triggered, the controlling player chooses which one of the duplicates to keep; the rest are put into their owners' graveyards (note: each goes to its own owner's graveyard, not necessarily the controller's, in case of effects like theft that let one player control another player's legendary permanent).
- Because it's a state-based action, if you gain control of, or a permanent becomes legendary such that you end up with two legendaries of the same name, this is checked and resolved before anyone gets priority again — there's no window to respond to it.

This applies the same way regardless of how many players are in the game, since it's based on what a single player controls, not on turn order or opponents generally; no multiplayer-specific rule is provided that changes this.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature dies the moment the game next checks state-based actions, not the instant the damage is marked. Damage dealt by a source without wither or infect is simply marked on the creature [302.7, 120.6]; that marking itself doesn't destroy anything — "Damage dealt to a creature... doesn't destroy it. Rather, state-based actions may destroy a creature... due to the results of the damage dealt" [120.5]. If the total damage marked on a creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, it "has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed" as a state-based action [704.5g, 302.7, 120.6].

State-based actions don't use the stack and aren't something players do — they're performed automatically before any player is given priority [704.1, 405.6f, 117.2d]. Specifically, every time a player would receive priority, the game checks for state-based actions first, performs any that apply, then repeats the check until none apply, and only then does a player actually get priority [704.3, 117.5]. So: if the lethal damage was dealt during the resolution of a spell or ability, the creature is NOT destroyed mid-resolution — state-based actions ignore what's happening inside a resolving spell/ability [704.4] — it's destroyed right after that spell or ability finishes resolving, as part of the state-based action check that happens before the next priority is given [704.3, 117.5]. If the damage was combat damage, damage-triggered abilities go on the stack and then the active player gets priority [510.3a], with the state-based action check (and thus the destruction) happening just before that priority is handed out [704.3].

This process is the same regardless of how many players are in the game — rule 704.3's priority-triggered SBA check isn't limited to two-player games. One exception worth noting: normally no player gets priority during the cleanup step, but if lethal damage is marked going into cleanup, the game still checks state-based actions at the start of that step and will destroy the creature then, before priority (if any) is given [514.3a, 704.3]. Also remember that at the end of the turn, during cleanup, all damage marked on permanents is removed [514.2, 703.4p], so a creature that survived the state-based action check with sub-lethal damage doesn't carry that damage into the next turn — but if it already had lethal damage marked, it's destroyed before that damage-removal step matters.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
By default, no — the rules only give you permission to cast your commander (say, Atraxa, Praetors' Voice) from the command zone, not from exile. Rule 903.8 states "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone," and that's the only casting permission the Commander rules grant for commanders. There's no blanket rule letting you cast a commander straight out of exile.

However, there are two wrinkles: 1) If your commander is put into exile, rule 903.9a is a state-based action that lets its owner move it into the command zone once state-based actions are checked — but that word "may" makes it optional, not mandatory. So if you want to, you can leave your commander sitting in exile instead of returning it to the command zone. 2) If some other effect (not the commander rules themselves) specifically grants you permission to cast spells from exile — for example, an effect that exiles a card and lets you cast it later — then you can use that separate permission to cast your commander while it's in that exile zone, following the normal requirements in [601.3e] and [601.3f] (you need a rule or effect that actually allows the cast, and nothing prohibiting it). If the card was exiled face down, [406.3b] additionally requires that you be allowed to look at that face-down card, and the resulting spell must match whatever qualities the effect specifies, in order to cast it.

One important consequence: casting your commander this way, from exile via some other effect, does NOT trigger the "commander tax" of [903.8], since that extra {2}-per-previous-cast cost is tied specifically to casting "from the command zone." Casting from exile is a different zone, so that tax doesn't apply to that particular cast (though it would still apply to future casts made from the command zone, counting all previous times you cast that commander from the command zone).

This answer holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — nothing in the cited rules about commanders returning to the command zone or being cast varies by player count.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer:
During the cleanup step (the second and final step of the ending phase), a fixed sequence of turn-based actions happens automatically, and normally no player gets priority at all.

The sequence is: First, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard down to that number [514.1]. This is a turn-based action and doesn't use the stack. Second, simultaneously, all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end [514.2][703.4p]. Also, as with any step ending, any unspent mana left in players' mana pools would empty [500.5][703.4q] (this actually happens as the step ends, per the general end-of-step rule).

Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3]. It's one of only two steps in the game (along with the untap step) where players don't normally get priority, and it ends as soon as all its specified actions are completed [500.3].

There is an exception, though: after the discard and damage-removal actions happen, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities (including ones that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step") are waiting to be put on the stack. If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and then the active player gets priority — players can cast spells and activate abilities normally. Once the stack is empty and everyone passes in succession, an entirely new cleanup step begins from the top [514.3a][704.3]. If nothing like that is pending, no player gets priority and the cleanup step simply ends [704.3].

This two-player-framed rule set doesn't call out any different behavior for cleanup steps in multiplayer games, so the mechanics described apply the same way regardless of player count.

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer:
State-based actions (SBAs) are checked automatically every time a player would receive priority – they are not tied to a fixed clock or a specific phase, but to the priority system itself. Under rule 704.2, SBAs are checked continuously and aren't controlled by any player. Rule 117.5 (echoed in 704.3) spells out the exact sequence: each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable SBAs as a single simultaneous event; if any were performed, the check repeats. Once a check produces no SBAs, any triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, and then the check for SBAs repeats again. This loop continues until a check occurs where no SBAs are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting — only then does the player actually receive priority (704.3, 117.5, 405.6f).

A few important wrinkles:
- SBAs are always checked before turn-based actions' priority window opens, but turn-based actions themselves (like the discard-to-hand-size action in 514.1, or draw-step actions) are handled first when a step/phase begins, before SBAs are checked and before triggered abilities go on the stack (703.3, 117.2c/d, 405.6e).
- During the cleanup step, players normally don't get priority at all. But the game still checks whether any SBAs would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting; if so, those SBAs are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and then (and only then) the active player gets priority (514.3a, 704.3).
- When an effect ends the turn or ends the combat phase (e.g., a card like Mandate of Peace ending combat), the rules explicitly deviate from normal resolution: SBAs are checked, but no player gets priority afterward and no triggered abilities are put on the stack at that point (724.1c, 724.2c).
- SBAs never use the stack (704.1, 704.1a) and are distinct from triggered abilities, which watch for game states but must still be put on the stack through the normal priority-granting process (704.1a, 603.1).

This all applies regardless of how many players are in the game — the priority/SBA-check loop described in 704.3 and 117.5 isn't stated as changing in multiplayer, so the same checking process applies whether there are two players or more.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply whoever's turn it is right now [102.1], [Active Player]. There's only ever one active player at a time (or, in the case of a game using the shared team turns option, one active team) — everyone else at the table is a nonactive player.

In a standard game (two-player or multiplayer without shared team turns), you determine the active player by tracking whose turn is currently being played: as turns pass around the table in turn order, the player currently taking their turn is the active player. During that player's combat phase, they're also specifically called the attacking player, and in a two-player game the other player is the defending player [506.2], [506.2b].

If the game uses the shared team turns option (mandatory in Two-Headed Giant and Archenemy), the concept shifts to teams: the team whose turn it is is the active team, and the other team(s) are nonactive teams [805.4a]. Within that active team, any of its members can be treated as making choices together (in whatever order they like) before nonactive teams act [805.6].

One subtlety: some abilities refer generically to "the active player" even when, due to a specific effect, that phrase could be ambiguous. In those cases, the ability's controller gets to choose which specific active player is meant when the effect is applied — this refers to one specific active player, not to all of them [805.9]. This mostly matters in unusual rules interactions, not day-to-day play.

So in short: check the turn structure — whoever's turn it currently is (or whichever team's turn it is, under shared team turns) is the active player/team.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?

2) Every turn thereafter (including the turn it enters), as a turn-based action: Immediately after a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control that has one or more chapter abilities [714.3c][703.4f]. This is a turn-based action, so it happens automatically without using the stack [714.3c][703.4f]. Rule 505.4 confirms this is the second thing that happens in the precombat main phase for the active player if they control one or more Sagas [505.4].

Note on read ahead: if a Saga with read ahead entered this turn, its chapter abilities can't trigger this turn unless the lore-counter count exactly matches the chapter symbol's number, per the read-ahead rule itself [702.155a].

Separately, whenever the number of lore counters on a Saga with chapter abilities becomes greater than or equal to its final chapter number (and it isn't currently the source of an unresolved triggered chapter ability), a state-based action forces its controller to sacrifice it [714.4][704.5s]. This check happens continuously, not just during the main phase, but it's a consequence of lore counters being placed rather than another time counters are added.

This works the same whether there are two players or more than two, since the timing rule refers only to the Saga's controller's own precombat main phase, with no dependency on number of opponents.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect—generated when a spell or ability resolves, or when a replacement effect is applied, or by a static ability that lets a player take an action—that does something at a later time rather than immediately. Like other triggered abilities, its text will contain "when," "whenever," or "at," even though that word usually won't begin the ability's printed wording.

Key points about how delayed triggered abilities work:
- They are created during the resolution of a spell or ability, as a result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action [603.7, 603.7a].
- A delayed triggered ability won't actually trigger until it has been created, even if the event it watches for happened just beforehand; and if the triggering event becomes impossible before the ability is created (e.g., the referenced object leaves the battlefield before the creating spell resolves), the ability simply never triggers [603.7a].
- Unless it has a stated duration (like "this turn"), it triggers only once, the next time its trigger event occurs; if the event happens more than once simultaneously, its controller chooses which occurrence causes it to trigger [603.7b].
- It still affects the object it refers to even if that object's characteristics change, but not if the object has left the zone it was expected to be in by the time the ability resolves (since a card that changes zones becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence) [603.7c, 400.7].
- Its source and controller are determined by what created it: a spell (603.7d), another activated/triggered ability (603.7e), a static ability generating a replacement effect (603.7f), or a static ability allowing an action (603.7g).
- A special subset, "reflexive triggered abilities," behave like delayed triggered abilities but are checked immediately upon creation, triggering based on whether their event already happened during the resolution of the ability that created them [603.12].
- Once triggered, a delayed triggered ability is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, becoming an object on the stack with only the text of that ability [603.3a].

This is the Comprehensive Rules Glossary definition, cross-referenced to rule 603.7 and its subrules, plus rule 610.2 which notes that many one-shot effects create delayed triggered abilities to do something later rather than as part of the immediate resolution.

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer:
Yes. Non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities, though most of the text on them is a special kind called a "spell ability." Rule [113.3a] states that any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability unless it's an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria described in rule [113.6]. Spell abilities are simply the instructions followed while the instant or sorcery spell is resolving.

Beyond spell abilities, instants and sorceries can also carry static abilities that specifically work while the spell is on the stack or in the zone it's cast from. Rule [604.5] notes that some static abilities apply while a spell is on the stack — commonly abilities about countering the spell, "additional cost to cast" abilities, "you may pay [cost] rather than pay this object's mana cost" abilities, and "you may cast this without paying its mana cost" abilities all work on the stack. Rule [113.6e] adds that an ability restricting or modifying how a particular object can be cast functions in any zone it could be cast from (usually the hand) and also on the stack. Rule [604.6] covers similar text like "You may cast [this card] . . . ," "You can't cast [this card] . . . ," or "Cast [this card] only . . . ," which apply in whatever zone you could cast the card from.

Characteristic-defining abilities (a subtype of static ability, per [604.1] and [604.3]) function in every zone, including the stack, hand, graveyard, etc., since they define an object's characteristics no matter where it is.

What instants and sorceries generally do *not* have are activated or triggered abilities that function while the spell itself is on the battlefield, simply because instants and sorceries don't stay on the battlefield — but a spell could still trigger an ability elsewhere or have a triggered/static ability worded to apply on the stack, consistent with [113.6].

This analysis doesn't turn on player count, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer: Yes. Split second only stops players from casting spells or activating abilities that aren't mana abilities — mana abilities are explicitly exempt. Rule [702.61a] defines split second as "players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities" while the spell with split second is on the stack, and [702.61b] confirms directly: "Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack." This is consistent with the general rule that a player may activate a mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they're casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment — even in the middle of casting or resolving something else ([117.1d], [605.3a]). Mana abilities also don't use the stack and resolve immediately ([113.4], [605.3b], [405.6c]), so they aren't blocked by split second's stack-based restriction in the first place. This holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since nothing about split second or mana abilities changes based on player count.
